The evidence on whether hypnotherapy works for smoking cessation is genuinely conflicting. Several randomized controlled trials support its effectiveness: one RCT found hypnotherapy patients were over three times more likely than NRT patients to abstain at 26 weeks post-discharge (RR=3.6; p=0.03) [d1][d2], and a separate study found that hospitalized patients who had one hypnotherapy session were more likely to be nonsmokers at 6 months compared with NRT-only or cold-turkey patients [d4]. Time magazine also notes that clinical research has shown hypnosis can aid smoking cessation [d7]. However, a Cochrane review of nine small trials found hypnotherapy no more effective than other behavioral interventions, and concluded there is "no evidence to support that hypnosis per se has any effect as an aid to smoking cessation" [d6]. Similarly, the American Cancer Society states there isn't enough evidence to show hypnotherapy works, and it is listed among the least successful quit methods [d8]. A health review site notes that while some recent studies are supportive, "research into hypnosis for smoking cessation is limited, so currently there's not enough evidence to confirm the benefits of hypnosis for smoking cessation definitively" [d5]. In summary, some RCTs suggest benefit—particularly in hospitalized patients—but major systematic reviews and health authorities have not found sufficient evidence to endorse hypnotherapy as a proven smoking cessation tool [d1][d2][d6][d8].
